chapter_text:
CHAPTER 21 - REPRODUCTION AND POPULATION CONTROL

Introduction

Reproduction is the biological process by which living organisms produce new individuals of their own kind. It ensures the continuity of a species from one generation to the next and is a defining feature of all living things. Human beings reproduce sexually: a new individual arises from the fusion of two specialised sex cells, or gametes - a sperm from the male and an ovum (egg) from the female. Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two parents, producing variation among offspring, which is the raw material of evolution. This chapter describes the human male and female reproductive systems, the formation of gametes (spermatogenesis and oogenesis), the menstrual cycle and its hormonal control, fertilization and the development of the embryo, the role of the placenta, birth and lactation, reproductive health, the control of human population through contraception, common sexually transmitted diseases including HIV/AIDS, and the assisted reproductive technologies that help infertile couples.

21.1 THE MALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM

The male reproductive system consists of a pair of testes, a system of ducts (epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra), accessory glands, and the external genitalia (penis and scrotum).

The TESTES are the primary male sex organs. They are a pair of oval bodies that lie outside the abdominal cavity in a pouch of skin called the SCROTUM. The scrotum keeps the testes at a temperature about two to three degrees below body temperature, which is essential for normal sperm formation. Each testis is packed with several hundred coiled SEMINIFEROUS TUBULES, the sites where sperms are produced. The walls of these tubules contain germ cells that divide to form sperms, and large SERTOLI CELLS that nourish and support the developing sperms. Between the tubules lie the interstitial cells of Leydig, which secrete the male sex hormone TESTOSTERONE. Testosterone controls the development of the male reproductive organs and the secondary sexual characters such as a deep voice, facial and body hair, and muscular growth.

Sperms formed in the seminiferous tubules pass into the EPIDIDYMIS, a long coiled tube on the surface of each testis where sperms mature and are stored. From the epididymis, sperms travel through the VAS DEFERENS (sperm duct), a muscular tube that carries them upward into the abdomen and joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the URETHRA. The urethra runs through the PENIS and serves as a common passage for both urine and semen.

Three sets of ACCESSORY GLANDS add secretions to the sperms to form SEMEN. The paired SEMINAL VESICLES secrete a fluid rich in fructose that provides energy for the sperms. The PROSTATE GLAND adds an alkaline secretion that neutralises the acidity of the female tract and activates the sperms. The paired bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands secrete a lubricating fluid. Semen is thus a mixture of sperms and these glandular secretions.

SPERMATOGENESIS is the process of formation of sperms in the seminiferous tubules. It begins at puberty and continues throughout life. The undifferentiated germ cells (spermatogonia) are diploid. Some of them enlarge to form primary spermatocytes, which undergo the first meiotic division to form two haploid secondary spermatocytes. Each secondary spermatocyte undergoes the second meiotic division to form two spermatids. Thus one primary spermatocyte gives rise to four haploid spermatids. The spermatids then change in shape and structure (a process called spermiogenesis) to become mature sperms. The hormones FSH and LH from the pituitary and testosterone from the testis regulate this process.

A mature SPERM (spermatozoon) is a microscopic, motile cell with three parts. The HEAD contains the haploid nucleus capped by an ACROSOME, a cap filled with enzymes that help the sperm penetrate the egg. The MIDDLE PIECE is packed with mitochondria that supply energy for movement. The TAIL is a long flagellum that lashes to propel the sperm forward. Millions of sperms are released in a single ejaculation, but only one fertilises the egg.

21.2 THE FEMALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM

The female reproductive system consists of a pair of ovaries, a pair of fallopian tubes (oviducts), the uterus, the vagina and the external genitalia.

The OVARIES are the primary female sex organs, a pair of almond-shaped bodies in the lower abdomen. They perform two functions: they produce the female gametes (ova) and they secrete the female sex hormones ESTROGEN and PROGESTERONE. Within each ovary are numerous ovarian follicles, each containing an immature egg. Estrogen controls the development of female reproductive organs and the secondary sexual characters, while progesterone prepares and maintains the uterus for pregnancy.

The FALLOPIAN TUBES or OVIDUCTS are a pair of tubes that carry the egg from the ovary towards the uterus. The funnel-shaped end near the ovary has finger-like fimbriae that collect the released egg. FERTILIZATION normally takes place in the upper part of the fallopian tube.

The UTERUS or womb is a hollow, muscular, pear-shaped organ in which the embryo develops during pregnancy. Its thick muscular wall is the myometrium and its inner glandular lining is the ENDOMETRIUM, which thickens each month to receive a fertilised egg. The lower narrow part of the uterus, the CERVIX, opens into the VAGINA, a muscular canal that receives the sperms during mating and serves as the birth canal.

OOGENESIS is the formation of the female gamete in the ovary. Unlike spermatogenesis, it begins before birth. In the foetal ovary, germ cells form millions of primary oocytes, which then enter a prolonged resting stage of meiosis. At puberty only a fraction remain. In each cycle a primary oocyte completes the first meiotic division to form one large secondary oocyte and a tiny polar body; the unequal division conserves cytoplasm for the egg. The secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and completes the second meiotic division only if a sperm enters it. Thus one primary oocyte forms just one functional ovum and two or three polar bodies.

The OVUM (egg) is one of the largest cells in the body, a rounded non-motile cell rich in cytoplasm and stored food. It is surrounded by a jelly-like membrane, the zona pellucida, and a layer of follicle cells. The stored nutrients support the early development of the embryo before it implants.

21.3 THE MENSTRUAL CYCLE

In human females the reproductive cycle is called the MENSTRUAL CYCLE. It is a roughly 28-day cycle of changes in the ovary and the uterus, controlled by hormones, that repeats from puberty (menarche) until menopause, pausing during pregnancy. The cycle has four phases.

The MENSTRUAL PHASE (about days 1-5) begins the cycle. If the egg is not fertilised, the thickened uterine lining breaks down and is shed along with blood through the vagina - this bleeding is menstruation.

The FOLLICULAR or PROLIFERATIVE PHASE (about days 6-13) follows. FOLLICLE STIMULATING HORMONE (FSH) from the pituitary stimulates an ovarian follicle to grow and mature. The growing follicle secretes ESTROGEN, which causes the endometrium to repair and thicken again in preparation for a possible pregnancy.

OVULATION (about day 14) is the release of the mature egg from the ovary into the fallopian tube. It is triggered by a sudden surge of LUTEINISING HORMONE (LH) from the pituitary, itself brought on by the peak of estrogen.

The LUTEAL or SECRETORY PHASE (about days 15-28) follows ovulation. The empty follicle becomes a yellow body, the CORPUS LUTEUM, which secretes PROGESTERONE (and some estrogen). Progesterone maintains the thick, glandular endometrium ready for implantation. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the lining is shed, beginning the next cycle. If pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum persists and progesterone keeps the lining intact. The interplay of FSH, LH, estrogen and progesterone thus coordinates the ovarian and uterine events of the cycle.

21.4 FERTILIZATION, PREGNANCY AND DEVELOPMENT

FERTILIZATION is the fusion of a sperm with the secondary oocyte to form a diploid ZYGOTE. It occurs in the upper part of the fallopian tube. Of the millions of sperms deposited, only one penetrates the egg; its entry triggers the completion of meiosis in the egg and the two haploid nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number of 46 chromosomes and determining the sex of the child (an X-bearing sperm gives a girl, a Y-bearing sperm a boy).

The zygote begins to divide repeatedly (cleavage) as it travels down the tube, forming a solid ball of cells (morula) and then a hollow ball, the BLASTOCYST. About a week after fertilization the blastocyst reaches the uterus and IMPLANTS - it embeds itself in the thick endometrium. This marks the beginning of pregnancy. The inner cell mass of the blastocyst develops into the EMBRYO, while the outer cells help form the placenta and membranes.

The developing human is called an EMBRYO for the first two months, during which the major organs form, and a FOETUS thereafter, when it grows and matures. Human pregnancy (GESTATION) lasts about nine months (280 days).

The PLACENTA is a disc-shaped organ that forms the intimate connection between the foetus and the mother's uterine wall. The foetus is joined to the placenta by the UMBILICAL CORD. In the placenta the blood of the foetus and the mother flow close together (but do not mix), allowing exchange across a thin barrier. The FUNCTIONS OF THE PLACENTA are: to supply oxygen and nutrients (glucose, amino acids) from the mother to the foetus; to remove carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes from the foetus to the mother; and to act as an endocrine gland secreting hormones such as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), estrogen and progesterone that maintain the pregnancy.

PARTURITION is the process of childbirth (delivery) at the end of gestation. It is brought about by strong rhythmic contractions of the uterine muscle, stimulated by the hormone OXYTOCIN from the pituitary. The contractions push the baby out through the cervix and vagina, and the placenta (afterbirth) is expelled shortly after.

LACTATION is the secretion of milk by the mother's mammary glands to feed the newborn. Milk production is stimulated by the hormone PROLACTIN, and its release (let-down) by oxytocin. The first milk, COLOSTRUM, is rich in antibodies that protect the infant against infection.

21.5 CONTRACEPTION AND POPULATION CONTROL

A rapidly growing human population strains food, water, housing, education, health services and the environment. POPULATION CONTROL through family planning aims to check the birth rate so that population growth stays in balance with available resources. The chief means of limiting family size is CONTRACEPTION - the deliberate prevention of pregnancy - together with raising the age of marriage, education (especially of girls), and awareness programmes.

CONTRACEPTIVE METHODS fall into several categories.

NATURAL METHODS avoid the meeting of sperm and egg without drugs or devices. They include the rhythm (safe-period) method, in which intercourse is avoided around the time of ovulation, and withdrawal (coitus interruptus). They are free of side effects but not very reliable.

BARRIER METHODS physically prevent sperms from reaching the egg. The CONDOM is a thin sheath worn over the penis; the diaphragm and cervical cap cover the cervix in the female. Condoms have the added advantage of protecting against sexually transmitted infections.

INTRAUTERINE DEVICES (IUDs) are small devices, such as the copper-T, placed inside the uterus by a doctor. They prevent implantation (and copper ones also reduce sperm motility), giving long-term protection.

HORMONAL METHODS use hormones to prevent ovulation. ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE PILLS containing estrogen and progesterone, taken daily, suppress the release of the egg. Injectable hormones and implants act similarly over longer periods.

SURGICAL METHODS (STERILISATION) give permanent contraception. In the male, VASECTOMY is the cutting and tying of the vas deferens so that sperms cannot enter the semen. In the female, TUBECTOMY is the cutting and tying of the fallopian tubes so that the egg cannot meet a sperm. These are safe and highly effective.

The choice of method depends on health, convenience, reliability and personal preference; a couple should consult a doctor.

21.6 REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH AND SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES

REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH means a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being in all matters relating to the reproductive system. It includes safe motherhood, proper nutrition and medical care during pregnancy, awareness of contraception, protection from sexually transmitted infections, and freedom from reproductive disorders. Sex education, counselling and access to health services are important for reproductive health.

SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES (STDs), also called sexually transmitted infections, are infections spread mainly through sexual contact. Common examples are gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, hepatitis-B and AIDS. Their symptoms may include sores, discharge, pain or, in some, no early sign at all. If untreated many STDs can cause infertility, damage to other organs, or transmission to the baby. Most bacterial STDs (like syphilis and gonorrhoea) can be cured with antibiotics if treated early; viral ones are harder to cure. Prevention includes avoiding unsafe sexual contact, using condoms, and prompt treatment.

AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by the HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS (HIV). HIV attacks and destroys the helper T-lymphocytes of the immune system, so the body gradually loses its ability to fight infections. HIV spreads through unprotected sexual contact with an infected person, through transfusion of infected blood, by sharing contaminated needles, and from an infected mother to her child during birth or breast-feeding. It does NOT spread by ordinary contact such as shaking hands, sharing food or mosquito bites. There is as yet no complete cure, but anti-retroviral drugs can control the virus and prolong life; awareness and prevention are the best defence.

INFERTILITY is the inability of a couple to conceive even after prolonged unprotected intercourse. It may be due to defects in the male, the female, or both - for example, low sperm count, blocked tubes, or hormonal problems. Many infertile couples can be helped by ASSISTED REPRODUCTIVE TECHNOLOGIES (ART). In IN-VITRO FERTILIZATION (IVF), popularly called the test-tube baby technique, eggs and sperms are collected and fertilization is carried out in the laboratory; an early embryo is then transferred to the uterus of the mother. Other techniques include artificial insemination and intra-uterine transfer of gametes or embryos. These technologies, used under proper medical and ethical guidance, allow many childless couples to have children.

SUMMARY

- Reproduction ensures the continuity of a species; humans reproduce sexually by the fusion of a sperm and an ovum.
- The male system: testes (in the scrotum) with seminiferous tubules produce sperms; epididymis, vas deferens and urethra carry them; seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands add secretions to form semen; testosterone controls male characters.
- Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules forms four haploid sperms from each primary spermatocyte; a sperm has a head (nucleus + acrosome), a mitochondria-rich middle piece and a tail.
- The female system: ovaries produce ova and secrete estrogen and progesterone; fallopian tubes carry the egg and are the site of fertilization; the uterus (with its endometrium) houses the embryo; the vagina is the birth canal.
- Oogenesis forms one functional ovum plus polar bodies; the ovum is a large, non-motile, food-rich cell.
- The menstrual cycle (about 28 days) has menstrual, follicular/proliferative, ovulatory and luteal/secretory phases, controlled by FSH, LH, estrogen and progesterone; ovulation occurs about day 14 at the LH surge.
- Fertilization in the fallopian tube forms a diploid zygote, which develops into a blastocyst and implants in the uterus; the embryo (then foetus) develops over about nine months.
- The placenta connects foetus and mother, exchanging nutrients, gases and wastes and secreting pregnancy hormones; parturition (by oxytocin) delivers the baby, and lactation (colostrum, by prolactin) nourishes it.
- Population control uses contraception - natural, barrier, IUDs, hormonal pills and surgical methods (vasectomy, tubectomy) - along with education and a higher age of marriage.
- Reproductive health covers well-being, safe motherhood and protection from STDs; AIDS (HIV) destroys immune cells and has no cure yet; infertility can often be treated by assisted reproductive technologies such as IVF.

key_takeaways: Humans reproduce sexually; the male testes make sperms and testosterone, the female ovaries make ova and the hormones estrogen and progesterone.
Spermatogenesis yields four sperms per primary spermatocyte, while oogenesis yields one functional ovum plus polar bodies.
The menstrual cycle's four phases are controlled by FSH, LH, estrogen and progesterone; an LH surge triggers ovulation about day 14.
Fertilization occurs in the fallopian tube; the blastocyst implants in the uterus and develops using the placenta over about nine months.
The placenta exchanges nutrients, gases and wastes and secretes hormones; oxytocin drives childbirth and prolactin drives milk production.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Reproduction and Population Control (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer short-answer questions in a few sentences and long-answer questions in detail with labelled points where asked.

questions.question: Name the site of sperm production in the testis and state the function of the Leydig cells.
questions.answer: Sperms are produced in the seminiferous tubules of the testis. The interstitial cells of Leydig, which lie between the tubules, secrete the male sex hormone testosterone. Testosterone controls the development of the male reproductive organs and the secondary sexual characters such as facial hair and a deep voice.
questions.explanation: Seminiferous tubules = site; Leydig cells = testosterone.

questions.question: Draw a labelled description of the three parts of a mature sperm and give the function of each.
questions.answer: A mature sperm has three parts. The HEAD carries the haploid nucleus and is capped by the acrosome, which contains enzymes that help the sperm penetrate the egg. The MIDDLE PIECE is packed with mitochondria that provide energy for movement. The TAIL is a long flagellum whose lashing propels the sperm forward towards the egg.
questions.explanation: Head (nucleus + acrosome), middle piece (mitochondria), tail (movement).

questions.question: State two functions of the ovary and name the two hormones it secretes.
questions.answer: The ovary performs two functions: (1) it produces the female gametes, the ova, and (2) it secretes the female sex hormones. The two hormones it secretes are estrogen, which controls the female reproductive organs and secondary sexual characters, and progesterone, which prepares and maintains the uterus for pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Produces ova + secretes estrogen and progesterone.

questions.question: Describe the four phases of the menstrual cycle and the hormones controlling each.
questions.answer: The menstrual cycle is a roughly 28-day cycle with four phases. (1) Menstrual phase (days 1-5): if the egg is not fertilised, the thick uterine lining breaks down and is shed with blood as menstruation. (2) Follicular or proliferative phase (days 6-13): FSH from the pituitary stimulates a follicle to grow; the follicle secretes estrogen, which repairs and thickens the endometrium. (3) Ovulation (about day 14): a surge of LH, triggered by peak estrogen, releases the mature egg from the ovary. (4) Luteal or secretory phase (days 15-28): the empty follicle forms the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to maintain the endometrium. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the lining is shed, starting the next cycle.
questions.explanation: Four phases + FSH, LH, estrogen, progesterone.

questions.question: Where does fertilization occur in humans and what is formed as a result?
questions.answer: Fertilization occurs in the upper part of the fallopian tube (oviduct). It is the fusion of a sperm with the secondary oocyte. As a result the two haploid nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote, which has the full set of 46 chromosomes and later develops into the embryo.
questions.explanation: Fallopian tube; forms diploid zygote.

questions.question: List three functions of the placenta.
questions.answer: The placenta (1) supplies oxygen and nutrients such as glucose and amino acids from the mother to the foetus; (2) removes carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes from the foetus to the mother; and (3) acts as an endocrine gland, secreting hormones such as hCG, estrogen and progesterone that maintain the pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Nutrition/gas supply, waste removal, hormone secretion.

questions.question: Explain the need for population control and describe any three methods of contraception.
questions.answer: A rapidly growing population strains food, water, housing, education, health services and the environment, so population control through family planning is needed to keep growth in balance with resources. Three contraceptive methods are: (1) Barrier methods, such as the condom, which physically stop sperms from reaching the egg and also guard against STDs. (2) Intrauterine devices (IUDs), such as the copper-T, placed in the uterus to prevent implantation and reduce sperm motility. (3) Hormonal pills containing estrogen and progesterone, taken daily to suppress ovulation. Other methods include natural (rhythm) methods and permanent surgical sterilisation (vasectomy in men, tubectomy in women).
questions.explanation: Need + three named methods with how they work.

questions.question: Distinguish between vasectomy and tubectomy.
questions.answer: Vasectomy is a male sterilisation method in which the vas deferens (sperm duct) is cut and tied, so that sperms cannot enter the semen. Tubectomy is a female sterilisation method in which the fallopian tubes are cut and tied, so that the egg cannot meet a sperm. Both are safe, permanent and highly effective methods of contraception.
questions.explanation: Vasectomy = vas deferens (male); tubectomy = fallopian tubes (female).

questions.question: Name the virus that causes AIDS and give two ways by which it spreads.
questions.answer: AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). It spreads by (1) unprotected sexual contact with an infected person and (2) transfusion of infected blood or sharing contaminated needles; it can also pass from an infected mother to her child. It does not spread by ordinary contact such as shaking hands.
questions.explanation: HIV; sexual contact and infected blood/needles.

questions.question: What is IVF and how does it help infertile couples?
questions.answer: IVF (in-vitro fertilization), popularly called the test-tube baby technique, is an assisted reproductive technology in which eggs and sperms are collected and fertilization is carried out in the laboratory outside the body. The early embryo formed is then transferred to the uterus of the mother, where it develops normally. IVF helps couples who cannot conceive naturally, for example because of blocked fallopian tubes or a low sperm count, to have a child.
questions.explanation: Lab fertilization + embryo transfer; helps blocked tubes/low count.

questions.question: Why are the testes located in the scrotum outside the body cavity?
questions.answer: The testes lie in the scrotum, outside the body cavity, so that they are kept at a temperature about two to three degrees below normal body temperature. This lower temperature is essential for the normal formation of sperms; if the testes were at full body temperature, sperm production would be impaired.
questions.explanation: Scrotum keeps testes cooler for sperm formation.

questions.question: Trace the path of a sperm from where it is formed to where it leaves the body.
questions.answer: A sperm is formed in the seminiferous tubules of the testis. It then passes into the epididymis, where it matures and is stored. From there it travels through the vas deferens (sperm duct) into the abdomen, joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, and enters the urethra. The urethra runs through the penis and carries the semen out of the body.
questions.explanation: Seminiferous tubules -> epididymis -> vas deferens -> ejaculatory duct -> urethra.

questions.question: Name the three accessory glands of the male reproductive system and state one function of each.
questions.answer: The three accessory glands are: (1) the seminal vesicles, which secrete a fructose-rich fluid that gives energy to the sperms; (2) the prostate gland, which adds an alkaline secretion that neutralises the acidity of the female tract and activates the sperms; and (3) the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands, which secrete a lubricating fluid. Together their secretions with the sperms form semen.
questions.explanation: Seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands with functions.

questions.question: Briefly describe the process of spermatogenesis.
questions.answer: Spermatogenesis is the formation of sperms in the seminiferous tubules, beginning at puberty. Diploid spermatogonia enlarge to form primary spermatocytes. Each primary spermatocyte undergoes the first meiotic division to form two haploid secondary spermatocytes, and each of these undergoes the second meiotic division to form two spermatids. Thus one primary spermatocyte gives four haploid spermatids, which then change shape to become mature sperms.
questions.explanation: Spermatogonia -> primary -> secondary spermatocytes -> spermatids (four) -> sperms.

questions.question: State the two main functions of the ovary.
questions.answer: The ovary has two main functions: (1) it produces the female gametes, the ova, by the process of oogenesis; and (2) it secretes the female sex hormones estrogen and progesterone, which control the female reproductive organs, the secondary sexual characters, and the preparation of the uterus for pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Produces ova; secretes estrogen and progesterone.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the human uterus.
questions.answer: The uterus (womb) is a hollow, muscular, pear-shaped organ in which the embryo develops. Its thick muscular wall is called the myometrium, and its inner glandular lining is the endometrium, which thickens each month to receive a fertilised egg. The narrow lower part of the uterus is the cervix, which opens into the vagina.
questions.explanation: Muscular pear-shaped organ; myometrium, endometrium, cervix.

questions.question: How does oogenesis differ from spermatogenesis in the number and size of gametes produced?
questions.answer: In spermatogenesis, one primary spermatocyte forms four equal, small, motile sperms. In oogenesis, one primary oocyte forms only one large, non-motile, food-rich ovum together with two or three tiny polar bodies that degenerate. The unequal divisions in oogenesis conserve cytoplasm and stored food for the single egg, whereas spermatogenesis produces many small gametes.
questions.explanation: Sperm: four small motile; ovum: one large plus polar bodies.

questions.question: Why is the ovum much larger than the sperm?
questions.answer: The ovum is much larger than the sperm because it stores a large amount of cytoplasm and food (yolk) that nourishes the early embryo before it implants in the uterus and obtains nutrients from the mother. The sperm, in contrast, needs only to carry the nucleus to the egg and be small and motile.
questions.explanation: Ovum stores food for the early embryo; sperm only carries nucleus.

questions.question: Name the four phases of the menstrual cycle in order.
questions.answer: The four phases of the menstrual cycle, in order, are: (1) the menstrual phase (days 1-5), (2) the follicular or proliferative phase (days 6-13), (3) ovulation (about day 14), and (4) the luteal or secretory phase (days 15-28).
questions.explanation: Menstrual, follicular/proliferative, ovulatory, luteal/secretory.

questions.question: Explain the roles of FSH and LH in the menstrual cycle.
questions.answer: FSH (follicle stimulating hormone) from the pituitary stimulates an ovarian follicle to grow and mature during the follicular phase; the growing follicle secretes estrogen. LH (luteinising hormone), also from the pituitary, surges around day 14 in response to peak estrogen and triggers ovulation, the release of the egg. LH also helps convert the empty follicle into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone.
questions.explanation: FSH matures the follicle; LH surge triggers ovulation and forms corpus luteum.

questions.question: Explain why the level of progesterone rises after ovulation and falls if pregnancy does not occur.
questions.answer: After ovulation the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone; this maintains the thick, glandular endometrium ready for implantation, so progesterone rises. If fertilization and pregnancy do not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates after about ten days, so it stops secreting progesterone and the level falls. The drop in progesterone causes the uterine lining to break down, producing menstruation and starting a new cycle.
questions.explanation: Corpus luteum makes progesterone; degenerates without pregnancy, so it falls.

questions.question: What is fertilization and where does it take place?
questions.answer: Fertilization is the fusion of a sperm with the secondary oocyte (egg) to form a diploid zygote. In humans it normally takes place in the upper part of the fallopian tube (oviduct). The fusion restores the full chromosome number of 46 and determines the sex of the child.
questions.explanation: Fusion of sperm and egg forming zygote; in the fallopian tube.

questions.question: Describe the changes from the zygote to implantation.
questions.answer: After fertilization the zygote begins to divide repeatedly by cleavage as it moves down the fallopian tube, first forming a solid ball of cells called the morula and then a hollow ball called the blastocyst. About a week after fertilization the blastocyst reaches the uterus and implants, embedding itself in the thick endometrium. Its inner cell mass forms the embryo, while the outer cells help form the placenta. Implantation marks the start of pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Zygote -> cleavage -> morula -> blastocyst -> implantation in uterus.

questions.question: How is the sex of a human child determined at fertilization?
questions.answer: The sex of a child is determined by the sex chromosome carried by the fertilising sperm. The egg always carries an X chromosome. If an X-bearing sperm fertilises the egg, the zygote is XX and develops into a girl; if a Y-bearing sperm fertilises it, the zygote is XY and develops into a boy. Thus the father's sperm decides the sex of the child.
questions.explanation: Egg is X; X-sperm gives girl (XX), Y-sperm gives boy (XY).

questions.question: What is the umbilical cord and what does it do?
questions.answer: The umbilical cord is the structure that joins the foetus to the placenta. It contains blood vessels that carry oxygen and nutrients from the placenta to the foetus and return carbon dioxide and wastes from the foetus to the placenta, so that these can be exchanged with the mother's blood.
questions.explanation: Cord links foetus to placenta; carries nutrients and wastes.

questions.question: What is parturition and which hormone brings it about?
questions.answer: Parturition is the process of childbirth, or delivery of the baby, at the end of gestation. It is brought about by strong, rhythmic contractions of the muscular wall of the uterus, which are stimulated by the hormone oxytocin from the pituitary gland. The contractions push the baby out through the cervix and vagina, and the placenta (afterbirth) is expelled soon after.
questions.explanation: Childbirth by uterine contractions stimulated by oxytocin.

questions.question: What is lactation and why is colostrum important?
questions.answer: Lactation is the secretion of milk by the mother's mammary glands to feed the newborn; it is stimulated by the hormone prolactin, with oxytocin causing milk release. The first milk secreted, called colostrum, is important because it is rich in antibodies that protect the infant against infections in the early days of life.
questions.explanation: Milk secretion (prolactin); colostrum gives antibodies.

questions.question: Why is population control necessary?
questions.answer: Population control is necessary because a rapidly growing population puts great pressure on food, water, housing, education, health services and the environment. If the number of people grows faster than the available resources, it leads to shortages, poverty and environmental damage. Family planning keeps population growth in balance with resources.
questions.explanation: Rapid growth strains resources; family planning balances it.

questions.question: Describe two barrier methods of contraception and one advantage they offer.
questions.answer: Two barrier methods are: (1) the condom, a thin sheath worn over the penis that stops sperms from entering the female tract; and (2) the diaphragm or cervical cap, which covers the cervix in the female to block sperms. A major advantage of barrier methods, especially the condom, is that besides preventing pregnancy they also protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.
questions.explanation: Condom and diaphragm; advantage - protect against STDs.

questions.question: Compare temporary and permanent methods of contraception with examples.
questions.answer: Temporary methods prevent pregnancy for a limited time and are reversible; examples include natural (rhythm) methods, barrier methods (condom, diaphragm), intrauterine devices (copper-T) and hormonal pills. Permanent methods are surgical sterilisations that give lasting contraception; these are vasectomy in men (cutting and tying the vas deferens) and tubectomy in women (cutting and tying the fallopian tubes). Temporary methods suit couples who may want children later, while permanent methods suit those who have completed their family.
questions.explanation: Temporary (reversible) vs permanent (surgical sterilisation) with examples.

questions.question: Name three sexually transmitted diseases and state how their spread can be prevented.
questions.answer: Three sexually transmitted diseases are gonorrhoea, syphilis and AIDS. Their spread can be prevented by avoiding unsafe or unprotected sexual contact, by using condoms during intercourse, by using only screened blood and sterile needles, and by getting prompt medical treatment for any infection. Awareness and sex education are also important preventive measures.
questions.explanation: Gonorrhoea, syphilis, AIDS; prevention by safe practices and awareness.

questions.question: What is infertility and name one assisted reproductive technology used to treat it.
questions.answer: Infertility is the inability of a couple to conceive a child even after prolonged unprotected intercourse; it may be due to problems in the male, the female or both, such as low sperm count or blocked fallopian tubes. One assisted reproductive technology used to treat it is IVF (in-vitro fertilization), the test-tube baby technique, in which fertilization is carried out in the laboratory and the embryo is transferred to the uterus.
questions.explanation: Inability to conceive; treated by IVF (ART).

questions.question: Describe the human male reproductive system with the functions of its main parts.
questions.answer: The human male reproductive system consists of the testes, a system of ducts, accessory glands and the penis. The testes are a pair of oval organs held in the scrotum outside the body, where a slightly lower temperature allows normal sperm formation. Each testis contains many coiled seminiferous tubules in which sperms are produced; Sertoli cells nourish the developing sperms, and the Leydig cells between the tubules secrete testosterone, the hormone that controls male organs and secondary sexual characters. Sperms pass into the epididymis, where they mature and are stored, then travel through the vas deferens and the ejaculatory duct into the urethra, which runs through the penis and carries semen out. Three accessory glands add secretions to form semen: the seminal vesicles supply fructose for energy, the prostate adds an alkaline sperm-activating fluid, and the bulbourethral glands add a lubricant. Together these parts produce, nourish, store and deliver sperms.
questions.explanation: Testes, ducts, glands, penis with functions.

questions.question: Describe the human female reproductive system and the process of oogenesis.
questions.answer: The human female reproductive system consists of a pair of ovaries, a pair of fallopian tubes, the uterus, the cervix and the vagina. The ovaries produce the ova and secrete estrogen and progesterone. Each fallopian tube carries the egg from the ovary towards the uterus; its funnel-shaped end has fimbriae that collect the released egg, and fertilization normally occurs in the upper tube. The uterus is a muscular, pear-shaped organ whose inner lining, the endometrium, thickens to receive the embryo; its lower part, the cervix, opens into the vagina, which is the birth canal. Oogenesis is the formation of the ovum. It begins before birth, when the foetal ovary forms millions of primary oocytes that then rest in meiosis. At puberty, in each cycle a primary oocyte completes the first meiotic division to form a large secondary oocyte and a tiny polar body. The secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and completes the second division only if a sperm enters it. Thus each primary oocyte forms only one functional, food-rich ovum plus polar bodies that degenerate.
questions.explanation: Female organs with functions + oogenesis.

questions.question: Analyse how the hormones FSH, LH, estrogen and progesterone coordinate the events of the menstrual cycle.
questions.answer: The menstrual cycle is coordinated by four hormones acting in sequence. During the follicular phase, FSH from the pituitary stimulates an ovarian follicle to grow. The growing follicle secretes estrogen, which repairs and thickens the endometrium and, as it peaks, feeds back on the pituitary to cause a sudden surge of LH. This LH surge triggers ovulation about day 14, releasing the egg. After ovulation, LH converts the empty follicle into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (and some estrogen). Progesterone maintains the thick, glandular endometrium so that it is ready for implantation, and it also suppresses further FSH and LH so that no new follicle matures. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone falls; the lining then breaks down as menstruation, and the fall in progesterone allows FSH to rise again, starting the next cycle. If pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum persists and progesterone stays high, so menstruation does not happen. Thus the rise and fall of these hormones, with their feedback loops, drive the orderly repeating phases of the cycle.
questions.explanation: Sequential FSH, estrogen, LH surge, progesterone with feedback.

questions.question: Explain the events from fertilization to the development of the foetus.
questions.answer: Fertilization is the fusion of a sperm with the egg in the upper fallopian tube, forming a diploid zygote with 46 chromosomes. As the zygote travels down the tube it divides repeatedly by cleavage, forming first a solid morula and then a hollow blastocyst. About a week after fertilization the blastocyst reaches the uterus and implants in the thick endometrium; this marks the beginning of pregnancy. The inner cell mass of the blastocyst develops into the embryo, while the outer cells help form the placenta and membranes. During the first two months the major organs of the body form, and the developing human is called an embryo; after two months it is called a foetus, and it grows and matures until birth. The placenta supplies it with nutrients and oxygen from the mother throughout this time. Human gestation lasts about nine months, after which the fully developed baby is born.
questions.explanation: Fertilization -> cleavage -> blastocyst -> implantation -> embryo -> foetus.

questions.question: Describe the structure and functions of the placenta.
questions.answer: The placenta is a disc-shaped organ that forms the intimate connection between the developing foetus and the mother's uterine wall. It develops partly from the outer cells of the blastocyst and partly from the uterine tissue. The foetus is joined to the placenta by the umbilical cord, which contains blood vessels. Within the placenta the blood of the foetus and the blood of the mother flow very close together but do not mix; exchange takes place across a thin barrier. The placenta has three main functions: (1) nutrition and respiration - it supplies oxygen and nutrients such as glucose and amino acids from the mother to the foetus; (2) excretion - it removes carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes from the foetus to the mother's blood for disposal; and (3) hormone secretion - it acts as an endocrine gland, producing hormones such as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), estrogen and progesterone that maintain the pregnancy. In this way the placenta serves the foetus as its lungs, gut, kidney and hormone source until birth.
questions.explanation: Disc-shaped organ, umbilical cord, no blood mixing; nutrition, excretion, hormones.

questions.question: Explain the various methods of contraception used for family planning.
questions.answer: Contraceptive methods used in family planning fall into several groups. (1) Natural methods avoid the meeting of sperm and egg without drugs or devices; they include the rhythm (safe-period) method, in which intercourse is avoided around ovulation, and withdrawal. They have no side effects but are not very reliable. (2) Barrier methods physically block sperms; the condom is worn over the penis, and the diaphragm or cervical cap covers the cervix. Condoms also protect against STDs. (3) Intrauterine devices (IUDs), such as the copper-T, are placed in the uterus by a doctor and prevent implantation, giving long-term protection. (4) Hormonal methods, such as oral pills containing estrogen and progesterone, are taken daily to suppress ovulation; injections and implants act similarly for longer. (5) Surgical methods (sterilisation) give permanent contraception: vasectomy cuts and ties the vas deferens in men, and tubectomy cuts and ties the fallopian tubes in women. The choice of method depends on health, reliability, convenience and whether the couple want children later; a doctor should be consulted.
questions.explanation: Natural, barrier, IUD, hormonal and surgical methods explained.

questions.question: Compare vasectomy and tubectomy as methods of contraception, and explain why they are considered permanent.
questions.answer: Vasectomy and tubectomy are both surgical methods of contraception, known as sterilisation. In vasectomy, performed on the male, a small part of each vas deferens (the sperm duct) is cut and the ends are tied. As a result, sperms produced in the testes can no longer pass into the semen, so the semen has no sperms to fertilise an egg, although the man's hormones and sexual function remain normal. In tubectomy, performed on the female, a part of each fallopian tube is cut and tied. This blocks the tube so that the egg released from the ovary cannot meet a sperm, and fertilization cannot take place. Both operations are safe and highly effective. They are considered permanent because the cut ducts or tubes are sealed and are not meant to be reopened; reversal, if attempted, is difficult and often unsuccessful. For this reason these methods are chosen mainly by couples who have completed their family and do not want more children.
questions.explanation: Both sterilisation; vas deferens vs fallopian tubes; permanent because ducts sealed.

questions.question: Describe AIDS: its cause, how it spreads, how it affects the body, and how it can be prevented.
questions.answer: AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is a serious sexually transmitted disease caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). HIV spreads mainly through unprotected sexual contact with an infected person, through transfusion of infected blood, by sharing contaminated needles and syringes, and from an infected mother to her child during birth or breast-feeding. It does not spread by ordinary contact such as shaking hands, sharing food or utensils, or by mosquito bites. Inside the body, HIV attacks and destroys the helper T-lymphocytes, the white blood cells that direct the immune response. As their numbers fall, the body gradually loses its ability to fight infections, so the person suffers repeated and severe illnesses that would normally be resisted. There is at present no complete cure, but anti-retroviral drugs can control the virus and prolong life. Prevention is therefore the best defence: avoiding unsafe sexual contact, using condoms, using only screened blood and sterile disposable needles, and spreading awareness and education about the disease.
questions.explanation: HIV cause, spread routes, destroys helper T-cells, prevention.

questions.question:

Rahul studies the testis under a microscope. He sees many coiled tubules, and between them larger cells. His teacher tells him the tubules make sperms and the cells between them make a hormone. He also learns that the testis is kept in a pouch of skin outside the body.

(a) Name the coiled tubules that make sperms.
(b) Name the cells between the tubules and the hormone they secrete.
(c) Name the pouch that holds the testis.
(d) Why is this pouch important for sperm formation?
questions.answer: (a) The coiled tubules are the seminiferous tubules. (b) The cells between the tubules are the Leydig (interstitial) cells, and they secrete the hormone testosterone. (c) The pouch is the scrotum. (d) The scrotum is important because it keeps the testes at a temperature about two to three degrees below body temperature, which is necessary for the normal formation of sperms.
questions.explanation: Seminiferous tubules, Leydig cells/testosterone, scrotum, cooler temperature.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A diagram of a sperm shows three regions: a pointed front carrying the nucleus with a cap, a short thick region behind it packed with mitochondria, and a long thread-like end.

(a) Name the three parts of the sperm.
(b) What is the cap on the front called and what is its function?
(c) Why does the middle region have many mitochondria?
(d) What is the function of the thread-like end?
questions.answer: (a) The three parts are the head, the middle piece and the tail. (b) The cap on the head is the acrosome; it contains enzymes that help the sperm penetrate the egg. (c) The middle piece has many mitochondria because they release the energy needed for the movement of the sperm. (d) The thread-like end is the tail (flagellum); its lashing movement propels the sperm forward towards the egg.
questions.explanation: Head/middle piece/tail; acrosome, mitochondria for energy, tail for movement.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

An egg is released from the ovary and picked up by finger-like projections. It then moves along a tube towards a pear-shaped organ whose lining has become thick.

(a) Name the finger-like projections.
(b) Name the tube along which the egg travels.
(c) Name the pear-shaped organ and its thick lining.
(d) In which part of the tube does fertilization usually occur?
questions.answer: (a) The finger-like projections are the fimbriae. (b) The tube is the fallopian tube (oviduct). (c) The pear-shaped organ is the uterus and its thick lining is the endometrium. (d) Fertilization usually occurs in the upper part of the fallopian tube.
questions.explanation: Fimbriae, fallopian tube, uterus/endometrium, upper tube.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A 28-day menstrual cycle is described. On about day 14 a hormone surges and the egg is released. Before this, another hormone from the pituitary had made a follicle grow, and the follicle had released a hormone that thickened the uterine lining. After the egg is released, the empty follicle changes into a yellow body.

(a) Name the hormone that surges on day 14 to release the egg.
(b) Name the pituitary hormone that makes the follicle grow.
(c) Name the hormone from the follicle that thickens the lining.
(d) Name the yellow body and the hormone it secretes.
questions.answer: (a) The hormone that surges on day 14 is LH (luteinising hormone). (b) The pituitary hormone that makes the follicle grow is FSH (follicle stimulating hormone). (c) The hormone from the follicle that thickens the lining is estrogen. (d) The yellow body is the corpus luteum, and it secretes progesterone.
questions.explanation: LH surge, FSH, estrogen, corpus luteum/progesterone.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A woman notices that her uterine bleeding begins about every 28 days but stops completely when she becomes pregnant.

(a) What is the shedding of the uterine lining as blood called?
(b) During which phase (days) of the cycle does this bleeding occur?
(c) Why does the lining break down when there is no pregnancy?
(d) Why does the bleeding stop during pregnancy?
questions.answer: (a) The shedding of the uterine lining as blood is called menstruation. (b) It occurs during the menstrual phase, about days 1-5 of the cycle. (c) When there is no pregnancy the corpus luteum degenerates and the level of progesterone falls, so the thick endometrium can no longer be maintained and it breaks down. (d) During pregnancy the corpus luteum persists and progesterone stays high, so the lining is maintained and is not shed; hence the bleeding stops.
questions.explanation: Menstruation, days 1-5, progesterone falls, progesterone stays high in pregnancy.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

After fertilization in the tube, the single cell divides again and again while moving towards the uterus. It becomes a hollow ball that then embeds itself in the uterine lining, and pregnancy begins.

(a) Name the single cell formed at fertilization.
(b) What is the repeated division called?
(c) Name the hollow ball of cells.
(d) What is the embedding of this ball in the uterine lining called?
questions.answer: (a) The single cell formed at fertilization is the zygote. (b) The repeated division is called cleavage. (c) The hollow ball of cells is the blastocyst. (d) The embedding of the blastocyst in the uterine lining is called implantation.
questions.explanation: Zygote, cleavage, blastocyst, implantation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Inside the uterus a disc-shaped organ connects the foetus to the mother's wall. Materials pass between the two bloodstreams without them mixing. At the end of nine months, strong contractions push the baby out, and after birth the mother feeds the baby with milk.

(a) Name the disc-shaped organ.
(b) Give two materials that pass from the mother to the foetus through it.
(c) Name the hormone that causes the contractions of childbirth.
(d) Name the first antibody-rich milk fed to the baby.
questions.answer: (a) The disc-shaped organ is the placenta. (b) Two materials that pass from the mother to the foetus are oxygen and nutrients such as glucose (or amino acids). (c) The hormone that causes the contractions of childbirth is oxytocin. (d) The first antibody-rich milk fed to the baby is colostrum.
questions.explanation: Placenta, oxygen/glucose, oxytocin, colostrum.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A newly married couple visit a clinic to learn about spacing their children. The doctor explains several temporary methods: one is a thin sheath worn during intercourse, one is a small copper device placed in the uterus, and one is a daily tablet of hormones.

(a) Name the thin sheath and one extra benefit it gives.
(b) Name the copper device and where it is placed.
(c) How does the daily hormone tablet prevent pregnancy?
(d) Give one reason a couple might prefer temporary methods over permanent ones.
questions.answer: (a) The thin sheath is the condom; besides preventing pregnancy it also protects against sexually transmitted infections. (b) The copper device is the copper-T (an intrauterine device), and it is placed inside the uterus. (c) The daily hormone tablet (oral contraceptive pill) contains estrogen and progesterone that suppress ovulation, so no egg is released to be fertilised. (d) A couple might prefer temporary methods because they are reversible, allowing the couple to have children later when they wish.
questions.explanation: Condom (+STD protection), copper-T in uterus, pill suppresses ovulation, reversible.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A couple who already have three children decide they do not want any more. The doctor describes two permanent operations: one for the man, in which a duct is cut and tied, and one for the woman, in which her tubes are cut and tied.

(a) Name the operation done on the man and the duct that is cut.
(b) Name the operation done on the woman and the tubes that are cut.
(c) Why can the man no longer father a child after his operation?
(d) Why are these methods called permanent?
questions.answer: (a) The operation on the man is a vasectomy, in which the vas deferens (sperm duct) is cut and tied. (b) The operation on the woman is a tubectomy, in which the fallopian tubes are cut and tied. (c) After a vasectomy the sperms can no longer pass into the semen, so the semen has no sperms and cannot fertilise an egg. (d) They are called permanent because the cut ducts or tubes are sealed and are not meant to be reopened; reversal is difficult and usually unsuccessful.
questions.explanation: Vasectomy/vas deferens, tubectomy/fallopian tubes, no sperms in semen, sealed ducts.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A health worker teaches a village about a viral disease that weakens the body's defences. She says the virus destroys certain white blood cells, spreads through infected blood and unprotected sex, but does not spread by shaking hands. She adds that a childless couple in the village were helped by a laboratory technique to have a baby.

(a) Name the disease and the virus that causes it.
(b) Which white blood cells does the virus destroy?
(c) Give one way the disease spreads and one way it does NOT spread.
(d) Name the laboratory technique that helped the childless couple.
questions.answer: (a) The disease is AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome), caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). (b) The virus destroys the helper T-lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). (c) It spreads through infected blood transfusion, sharing contaminated needles or unprotected sexual contact; it does NOT spread by shaking hands (or by sharing food or mosquito bites). (d) The laboratory technique is IVF (in-vitro fertilization), the test-tube baby technique.
questions.explanation: AIDS/HIV, helper T-lymphocytes, blood/sex vs handshake, IVF.
